analysis.one_liner: Restores net neutrality rules barring internet providers from blocking, throttling, or charging websites for fast lanes.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it was referred to committee in March 2019 and died there when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cancel the FCC's 2017 decision to stop regulating broadband as a public-utility-style service, and bring back the FCC's 2015 net neutrality rules. Those rules let the FCC police internet providers and ban blocking websites, slowing them down, or letting companies pay for faster delivery. The 116th Congress ended with the bill still sitting in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who get a legal guarantee that their provider cannot block or slow websites or force apps to pay extra to reach them at full speed. Small web businesses and startups also benefit because they compete on equal terms with large companies that could otherwise pay providers for priority delivery.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and small web businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the FCC's December 2017 'restoring internet freedom' order, which had ended the agency's authority over broadband and handed it to the Federal Trade Commission.

It restores the FCC's 2015 Open Internet order, which classifies both mobile and fixed broadband as telecommunications services under FCC authority, and brings back rules prohibiting blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization.
The bill prevents the FCC from simply reissuing the 2017 order in the same form unless Congress later passes a law specifically allowing it.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband and cable providers (Comcast, AT&T, Verizon, Charter and their peers) bear the cost: they would again be regulated by the FCC, barred from practices like paid prioritization, and subject to open-internet rules they had spent years getting removed.

drawbacks.text: Broadband providers argued that treating internet service like a 1930s telephone utility discourages investment in network upgrades, and consumers could ultimately see that in slower build-out or higher prices; the bill rejects this by statute rather than by finding a compromise framework.

The bill locks its rules in place — it forbids the FCC from issuing a substantially similar replacement for the 2017 order without new congressional authorization — which reduces flexibility for any future FCC, including one that might want to fix problems with the restored rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For internet users, the bill restores enforceable guarantees that providers cannot block, slow, or put a price tag on access to websites. The honest counterweight is the providers' investment argument, which has never been settled; but the bill's protection is real and its costs fall mainly on a handful of very large companies. On balance the benefit to ordinary users outweighs the cost, though the rigid statutory lock-in is a design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ed Markey introduced the Save the Internet Act on March 6, 2019, with 44 original cosponsors including the Senate's top Democrat, Chuck Schumer.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced.
The bill received 45 cosponsors — 43 Democrats and 2 independents — and no Republicans.
No further Senate action was ever recorded: the committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate never debated or voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The companion bill passed the House in April 2019, leaving the Senate as the chamber that never voted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major broadband providers came out ahead: the 2017 FCC order they favored stayed in force, broadband remained largely outside FCC authority, and no net neutrality rules were restored by statute.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the Senate's Democratic leadership and caucus behind it.

for.name: 45 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Schumer and every Senate Democrat who signed on.

for.name: House of Representatives
for.role: Passed the identical Save the Internet Act companion bill
for.what_they_did: Passed the House companion version in April 2019, sending the bill to the Senate with one chamber's approval.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for Senate floor time, even after the House passed its companion.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Broadband and cable industry
against.role: Internet service providers (Comcast, AT&T, Verizon, Charter and trade groups)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against restoring the 2015 Title II rules and against the 2017 repeal being overturned.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 Senate cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republicans signed on, and a Republican-controlled Senate never acted on the bill after the Democratic House passed its companion.

industries.note: The bill would reclassify broadband under FCC authority and bar blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization — practices that let providers extract payment from websites and control which services run well. Their gain from the bill failing was the public's cost in lost protections.

industries.industry: Internet content, streaming, and app platforms
industries.note: Net neutrality rules keep them from paying providers for priority access; without them, large platforms can afford the fees but startups and smaller sites cannot, tilting competition toward incumbents.
The restored rules guarantee that reaching customers online does not depend on negotiating with each internet provider, which is the mechanism that keeps low barriers to entry on the web.
